Readings / When does digital growth become durable use?
Reading

Does growth in electronic-money accounts and transactions represent durable voluntary financial use?

When does digital growth become durable use?

Report an error

Historical evidence from Yemen records a large base of e-money accounts by 2019 alongside dormancy, one-off use and a transaction mix still closely tied to cash. The open question is whether people choose to return to digital finance and find enough value to keep using it.

Evidence periodProvider data 2016–2019, from a 2020 study of five e-money providers · CBY-Aden payment reports 2024–2025 and the FMIIP baseline of January 2025, shown beside the historical data, not as a continuation
Last reviewed10 October 2026

What not to conclude

Registrations, accounts, one-time use, transaction growth and infrastructure expansion do not prove unique, repeat, voluntary or durable financial use.

The readingBefore reading scale as useWhat would change this reading?Trace and sourcesGo further

By December 2019, the five e-money providers covered by a study of the Institute of Banking Studies had 807,919 electronic-money accounts. The same study reports an average dormant or inactive share of 23%, and notes that some accounts were used only once, or because circumstances required it. This is not a paradox. The number of accounts establishes scale within the source universe. Dormancy and one-off use show why scale alone does not establish durable financial use.

An account can exist without becoming a relationship

Registration does not tell us whether an account was used once or repeatedly, whether use was voluntary or triggered by a payment someone else made, whether value stayed in the account, whether the user paid or saved with it, or whether the service became preferable to cash for any purpose.

What the money moved for

CauseWay’s grouping of a 2019 transaction table in the same study indicates that 57.03% of recorded e-money transaction value was cash-in or cash-out and 29.97% was movement between bank and electronic accounts; bills and purchases together were 2.41%. The grouping is CauseWay’s, not a headline in the source.

Cash-in and cash-out are not failed digital finance. Where moving value safely or easily is hard, that function has real economic use. But a system dominated by entry to and exit from cash tells us something different from repeated merchant, bill, saving or other digital use.

Useful before durable

The evidence supports neither extreme: that every new account proves inclusion, or that episodic use proves digital finance failed. A service can solve a real problem once and still not become a persistent financial relationship.

The historical provider evidence also reports strong urban concentration and a low share of women within its own universe. These are not 2026 national estimates. Their present value is to show what current measurement must test: who uses digital finance, not merely how many accounts exist.

Later counts exist, but they do not continue this series. For 2024 and 2025 the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) publishes counts of e-wallet subscribers, most recently 2,102,484 for the first half of 2025, with no published definition of a subscriber. The World Bank-financed Yemen Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project (FMIIP) records a January 2025 baseline of 375,252 active e-wallet accounts, counting an account as active if it was used for at least one financial transaction in the last 90 days. Neither count has been reconciled with the other, or with the 807,919 e-money accounts that five providers held in December 2019. Subscribers are not active accounts, and neither count is a number of people. The historical and current figures therefore sit side by side: the difference between them is not growth, decline, inactivity or a return to use, and no share of active or dormant accounts can be drawn from it.

Before reading scale as use

Before reading an account count as evidence of use, check what the count includes: registered accounts or active ones, and under what definition of “active”. Check the provider universe and the period: the historical figures here describe the providers in one study, not the market today. A transaction-value mix describes value, not how many people used the service or how often they returned.

What would change this reading?

Current data on unique active users, recency and frequency of use, what accounts are used for, value retained in the account, merchant and bill payments, dormancy, failed transactions, cost, complaints and provider-side behaviour, combined with demand-side questions on why people open an account, use it, return to it or stop. The measures that matter are registration, activity, recency, frequency, function, choice or trigger, quality and persistence, and they should not be read as an automatic ladder.

Scale tells us how large the digital system became. Return use tells us whether it entered financial life.

Related readings

Evidence periodWorld Bank and G2Px material, May 2024 · reference period of the recipient figure not recorded · Cash Consortium of Yemen study (2026) and report (May 2026) and World Bank project documents (2025–2026) · UNICEF press releases (October and December 2024) · Cash Consortium of Yemen survey of January 2024 (posted online November 2024)
The payment arrived. What happened next?
Material on Yemen’s digital-payment pilot describes transfers paid into fully functional accounts, with recipient choice, for 45,460 recipients, a count reported by the programme. That is an important step in delivery. It is not yet evidence that the accounts stayed part of recipients’ financial lives after the payments.
Evidence periodPoint-of-sale (POS) counts March 2025 – June 2026 · institutional records June–August 2026 · project results framework January 2025
When does a payment reform become financial inclusion?
A rule can be issued, infrastructure can expand, institutions can be created and transactions can appear while evidence on reach, repeated use, service quality, protection and outcomes remains incomplete. The question is how far a reform’s effects can actually be traced.
